question: The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) has been allowed to operate without any public accountability or transparency. The Article 3 arrangements under the EIOPA Regulation1 provide for behind closed doors, undocumented and off-the-record discussion with a limited number of MEPs – if the Chair of EIOPA agrees to attend.

These arrangements are the very antithesis of openness or transparency. My question to the Commission is regarding standards that should apply to EIOPA operations. At the time of her appointment, Commissioner Albuquerque indicated that ‘accountability and transparency are not only a requirement, they are a moral imperative’. 1.

Does the Commission believe that the accountability and transparency standards the Commissioner espoused should be an imperative for EIOPA, and more specifically, how is EIOPA held accountable to EU citizens?
Does the Commission believe that it should have the competence to review EIOPA failures in openness and transparency?
How are the highly restrained arrangements under Article 3 of the EIOPA Regulation compatible with the openness and transparency standards that the Commission espouses?
OJ L 331, 15.12.2010, pp. 48–83, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2010/1094/oj.
answer: The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) is accountable to the European Parliament and the Council and is subject to the transparency obligations laid down in the EIOPA Regulation (1).

Pursuant to Article 3, EIOPA is obliged to publish an annual report on its activities, and the EIOPA chairperson is obliged to participate in public hearings before the European Parliament on EIOPA’s performance, to report to the European Parliament in writing on EIOPA’s activities, including any relevant information requested by the European Parliament on an ad hoc basis, and to reply orally or in writing to any question addressed to it by the European Parliament or by the Council.

Only when professional secrecy and confidentiality obligations (2) are to be warranted, the European Parliament can request — and EIOPA is obliged to- hold confidential discussions with the Chair, Vice-Chairs and Coordinators of the competent committee of the European Parliament.

Article 3 of the EIOPA Regulation also refers to the European Parliament’s right to set up a temporary Committee of Inquiry as foreseen in Article 226 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). Article 1(6) of the EIOPA Regulation sets out that EIOPA will act independently and objectively and in the interests of the EU.

Given EIOPA’s status as an autonomous agency, it is for the European Parliament and the Council to exercise the abovementioned prerogatives. The Commission is committed to ensuring that the EIOPA Regulation is applied in full. The EIOPA Regulation sets accountability and transparency requirements, and the European Parliament and the Council have the prerogative to demand information and clarifications at any time.

OJ L 331, 15.12.2010, pp. 48-83, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2010/1094/oj. Namely Articles 3, 43a and 72 of EIOPA Regulation (EU) No 1094/2010. Pursuant Article 70 of EIOPA Regulation (EU) No 1094/2010 and Article 339 TFEU.
